The Federalist Papers. A series of essays written by James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, and John Jay between seventeen eighty-seven and seventeen eighty-eight, the Federalist Papers argued for ratification of the United States Constitution. Published under the pseudonym Publius and disseminated widely in newspapers, the essays defended the Constitution's structure of federal government, separation of powers, and system of checks and balances against critics who feared centralized authority.

Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay collaboratively wrote eighty-five essays, with Hamilton authoring the most at least fifty-one, Madison around fifteen, and Jay only five due to illness. The true authorship of some essays remained disputed for decades. The essays addressed specific constitutional controversies. Federalist Number Ten argued that the Constitution's large republic would moderate factional conflict and protect individual rights. Federalist Number Fifty-One explained the separation of powers and checks and balances.

Federalist Number Seventy-Eight, written by Hamilton, established the intellectual foundation for judicial review—the power of courts to strike down unconstitutional laws—later codified in Marbury versus Madison in eighteen hundred three. The essays were instrumental in securing ratification in key states, especially New York, where anti-Federalist opposition was fierce. They were reprinted as a collected volume shortly after ratification and have remained canonical texts of constitutional interpretation.

The Federalist Papers represent the most rigorous defense of representative republicanism and separation of powers produced during the founding era, drawing on Enlightenment political philosophy while addressing the specific circumstances of post-Revolutionary America. Legal scholars and Supreme Court justices continue to cite the Federalist Papers when interpreting constitutional clauses, treating the essays as authoritative evidence of the Framers' original intent.
